note: The redaction contract, run by the Dart suite and by crates/ripple-telemetry. Generated from the Dart Redactor and reviewed. See docs/specs/session-logs.md section 7.

cases.name: home becomes a tilde
cases.why: home goes before the username, or the folder names survive and the one part that was never secret is removed

cases.name: a project root wins over home
cases.why: registered at runtime; it is the folder somebody keeps unpublished work in

cases.name: the deepest project root wins
cases.why: sorted longest first, so a project nested in another is named for itself

cases.name: a bare username is mopped up afterwards
cases.why: the home rule has already dealt with where it actually appears
cases.in: the account ada has no write permission
cases.out: the account <user> has no write permission

cases.name: an email goes before the username
cases.why: most usernames are the local part of one

cases.name: a non-ASCII local part is still an email
cases.why: THE ASCII-class case. Dart \w is ASCII and Rust \w is Unicode-aware, so neither shorthand may be trusted; both spell the class out. This used to go into a log file untouched.

cases.name: so is one in a non-Latin script
cases.why: same rule, and the case a transliteration of either engine gets wrong

cases.name: a non-ASCII domain too
cases.why: this used to miss the email rule and then be caught by the username one, which replaced the local part and left the domain standing

cases.name: a username ending in a non-ASCII letter is still replaced
cases.why: the same trap one rule over: a word boundary after an accented letter is not a boundary at all, so this name was never redacted while `renée` was
cases.in: the account josé has no write permission
cases.out: the account <user> has no write permission

cases.name: and its home directory still becomes a tilde
cases.why: the home rule is a string replacement and never had the problem; this pins that the two agree

cases.name: a github token
cases.why: credentials go first of all, before another rule can cut one in half

cases.name: a github pat
cases.why: the newer prefix, documented and stable

cases.name: an api key
cases.why: the third documented prefix

cases.name: an authorization header keeps its scheme
cases.why: knowing which kind of credential was in hand is diagnostic; the value never is

cases.name: a named secret keeps its key
cases.why: the key admits what it is and that is the useful half

cases.name: url user info
cases.why: the two things before the at-sign

cases.name: a residual path keeps its basename
cases.why: a log that says <path> twelve times looks like evidence and is not

cases.name: an install directory is left standing
cases.why: which package is this? is the first thing anybody asks

cases.name: a url is not mangled into a path
cases.why: a preceding / or : means this is the tail of a URL

cases.name: an ip address goes
cases.why: says where somebody is

cases.name: a loopback stays
cases.why: identifies nobody and is the diagnosis for the local endpoint

cases.name: an ipv6 loopback stays too
cases.why: same argument

cases.name: a time of day is not an address
cases.why: at least three colons, so hh:mm:ss survives

cases.name: an empty string is not worth any of this
cases.why: the early return

cases.name: digits in another script are not an address
cases.why: the other half of the ASCII-class trap. Dart’s \d is ASCII so this is left alone; Rust’s \d is Unicode and would redact it, so the port spells the class [0-9]. Over-redaction rather than a leak, but a log that says <ip> about something that is not one is evidence that is not.

cases.name: an address touching a non-ASCII word is still an address
cases.why: THE case that makes (?-u:\b) load-bearing, and the one a naive port leaks on. Dart’s \b is ASCII, so there is a boundary between 連接 and the digits and the address is removed. Rust’s \b is Unicode-aware, so a transliteration finds no boundary, does not match, and writes the address down.
